column1: # cases.tsv - the assertions this suite makes, and what each one is called.
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Alexandre Gomes Gaigalas <alganet@gmail.com>
# SPDX-License-Identifier: ISC
# id <TAB> title <TAB> applies-to
# `applies-to` is a space separated list of lanes, or `*` for every lane. It is
# what turns a missing row into a reading: a case that applies to a lane and was
# never reported there is a hole, and until this file existed there was no way to
# tell that from a case nobody had written yet.
# Named lanes and not `*`, because no case here applies to all ten. With `*` the
# grid put a `-` in thirty-three cells for a lane that runs none of them, which is
# noise in the column that is supposed to carry the signal: `-` has to mean a lane
# that was expected to report and did not.
# That was written when four lanes reported nothing at all -- bsd, kde-live,
# wayland and macos-netinstall each ran one thing and none of it was this. Three
# of the four report now, and rather more than they did: all sixteen suites in
# netinstall/test speak this vocabulary, so bsd carries eight families off the
# reduced OpenBSD list, macos-netinstall carries eleven, and wayland carries the
# one it asks for. kde-live is still the only lane with no row anywhere here; it
# runs test/qtkde.sh and nothing else, and until that suite has a vocabulary it
# is a lane the registry has nothing to say about.
# A suite absent from here is not always one waiting to be converted, and the
# manifest is where the difference is written. test/fontflip.sh opens by calling
# itself a PROBE and its `fontflip` row carries `soft` on all three lanes that
# run it, which is test/run.sh's word for a step that reports a reading nobody
# asserts -- a red one is a lane that measured something, not a lane that failed.
# test/matrix.py says the other half of it: readings must not become cases,
# because every row in that grid is supposed to be something that can be true or
# false. So the empty `fontflip` column is the design and not a gap.
# Its `fontlive` row is a different matter: same script, `NT_FONTFLIP_LIVE_ONLY`
# set, and not soft, so what it exits with does reach the lane. Anyone converting
# that file has to decide what the soft row's rows would mean here first -- both
# rows run on gjs, and a probe filing a FAIL would redden a cell for a lane that
# deliberately does not count it.
# windows-launch was absent from the walk for a long time, because
# verify-windows.ps1 asserted the same facts in its own sentences and reported
# none of these ids. It is on them now: it writes the samples it was already
# taking as a record and hands that to test/lib/walk.sh, which is the shape
# verify-std.ps1 has used to reach test/lib/analyse.sh since the analysis moved
# there. Four lanes hold the walk now rather than three.
# walk.close.process-exits stays macOS's alone. It watches a *process* after the
# window is gone rather than a record, so there is nothing in the walk record for
# another lane to answer it from.
# The ids are dotted and start with the probe family, so a sheet sorts into the
# order somebody reads it in. They are stable across lanes on purpose -- three
# verifiers assert that a window reached 500x400 and until now spelled it three
# different ways, which made one fact look like three to sheetdiff.py.
# The launcher's own walk: neutrinotest.js drives it and verify-linux.sh,
# verify-macos.sh and verify-windows.ps1 each watch it on their own platform.

column1: # The engine walk, from test/lanes.sh -- which engine is chosen, and what a
# status coming back from one means.
# It runs on four lanes and needs no display on any of them: the candidates are
# stub interpreters that record having run and exit with a status the suite
# picks, because the walk's contract is "what does a status mean" and a stub can
# say a status a real interpreter can only be coaxed into. That is also why this
# family is on macos, which runs it from a step of its own rather than from the
# manifest: two of these name osascript, and until that step existed they were
# asserted only where osascript does not exist.
# Five of them are a skip on any given machine and never the same five, which is
# this family's whole shape. Whether a lane can hand its engine a document with
# no name is a property of the kernel -- Linux reopens an unlinked descriptor
# through /proc/self/fd and macOS cannot -- so lanes.qt.reached is asked exactly
# where the four lanes.handoff.* cases cannot be, and the other way round. Both
# arms are registered for all four lanes because both are real questions there;
# which one gets asked is the machine's answer, not the registry's.

column1: # The hostile document, from test/verify-attack.sh and test/verify-attack.ps1 --
# what a page that is trying to drive the native window gets, on the four lanes
# that can run one.
# windows-content is on these ids now, and it is the first family answered by a
# PowerShell suite in its own right rather than through a record handed to bash.
# verify-attack.ps1 was always the near-line-for-line twin of verify-attack.sh
# -- same probe, same settled-title protocol, same field names, comments that
# quote each other -- and it asserted every one of these facts in sentences of
# its own that no reader could line up with the other three lanes'. It speaks
# the six words now, so the twin pair answers one set of questions instead of
# two sets that happen to agree.
# Two of these are the escape itself rather than a residual, and they are why
# the suite exits where it finds them: a frame or a data: document whose title
# reached the window has already driven it, and nothing measured afterwards
# would be about the build under test. They were bare `FAIL:` lines and an
# `exit 1` before this, so the run that mattered most filed the least.
# Two more are asserted on one platform and recorded on the other, and the
# reason is in the suite: the macOS driver aims its navigation at a host that
# never resolves, so the provisional load fails on its own and every driver
# reports REFUSED whether it refused anything or not. That was a NOTE nothing
# read; it is a skip carrying the reason now, so the cell says which of the two
# it is. test/navrefuse.sh is where that question is asked against a target that
# answers.

column1: # The hostile navigation against a target that answers, from test/verify-nav.ps1.
# The attack family above asks this question too and cannot settle it: that page
# aims at a host that never resolves, so the load fails on its own and a driver
# with no guard reports the same REFUSED as one with. This suite serves a real
# page on a real port, which is the difference, and it is why attack.nav.refused
# carries the comment pointing here.
# windows-content alone. test/navrefuse.sh asks about a navigation refusal on
# macOS and shares two of these sentences, but not the apparatus: it patches the
# refusal line out of the artifact and compares the guarded build against the
# unguarded one, where this serves a target and reads what arrived at it. Two
# suites answering differently-shaped questions should not be made to share ids
# because two of their sentences agree -- that is the thing the ids were
# introduced to stop.
# nav.target.served is the control, and it is a case rather than a reading
# because the run is meaningless without it: a page that navigates into a closed
# port refuses nothing by having nothing to refuse. The two apparatus exits that
# used to end this suite -- no python, and nothing answering -- file it as a
# failure and skip the seven below, where before they exited 1 with no verdict
# at all.

column1: # The loader environment, from test/loaders.sh -- what the standalone launch
# path hands its engine, and what it must not.
# The suite is older than this vocabulary and said everything it had to say in
# prose: eleven PASS lines and fourteen failures, on four lanes, none of which
# reached a case id. It is the largest family here whose lanes disagree by
# design, and the disagreement is the toolkit rather than the machine.
# Which arm a lane is under is decided from the engine that actually came up and
# not from the lane's name, because three engines drive GTK now -- gjs, cjs and
# python3 -- and a lane matched on the string "gjs" would be put under Qt's
# expectations and asserted the opposite of the truth about it.
# So the pairs. compat.data-taken and boundary.data-arrives assert opposite
# things and each is registered only where it is true: the GTK lanes take the
# data names with their compatibility unset, and everywhere else those names
# have to arrive, because they name data and not code. The effect family splits
# the same way -- four of its knobs are GTK's, the renderer prefix is Qt's, and
# macos is registered for none of them, since osascript takes no insert at all
# and there is no "loaded without the fix" half to compare against.

column1: # The spec grammar, from netinstall/test/names.sh -- the third netinstall suite
# through the conversion, and the first where an id is not one assertion.
# That file makes about seventy of them, and most are one spec apiece: twelve
# reserved shapes, nine malformed names, six downloader markers, six pin lengths.
# Seventy rows here would be seventy rows of `.` in six of the ten columns, and
# they would say seventy times over the one thing this suite has to say -- that
# four lanes read the grammar the same way. So an id names the question and the
# sentence keeps the spec, which is what a reader of a red lane actually needs.
# Nothing is averaged away by that. test/matrix.py resolves a repeated id by
# letting FAIL win -- it has done since decoflip started reporting one case under
# two decoration settings -- so a family whose twelfth member broke is a red
# cell. Measured rather than assumed: asserting that shape 1 is reserved, which
# it is not, turns names.shape.reserved red on a lane where its other twelve
# members passed, whichever end of the list the failure is at.

column1: # The pin floor, from netinstall/test/pinfloor.sh. Same lanes again: the suite
# runs first in the netinstall list, and it is in the reduced OpenBSD one too,
# because a floor is a question about a parser and needs no webview.
# pinfloor.boundary is fourteen pin lengths under one id, for the reason
# names.sh groups: the sentence carries the length and the id carries the claim.
# 0, 1, 8, 15, 16, 17, 24, 31 and 65 and 80 must refuse; 32 through 64 must
# resolve. Both ends, so a floor that went up cannot pass by rejecting more than
# it was asked to -- measured by moving the expected floor to 33, which turns
# the cell red on the one length that changed.
# pinfloor.cause.distinct is the case this file is really about and it had no
# row at all before the conversion, because it spoke only when it failed. Before
# the floor moved, a pin below it was fetched and then failed the comparison --
# the same sentence a wrong pin produces -- so a suite asserting "this was
# refused" could not say which refusal it got. That it is now two refusals is
# what verify.pin.reason and names.pin.floor.reason rest on.
# The six `report:` lines this suite ends on stay readings and get no id. They
# say what the floor is rather than whether it held, and a reading in the grid
# would be a row that cannot be true or false.

column1: # What each platform leaves writable, from netinstall/test/writable.sh. The same
# four lanes again -- the netinstall suite without a shorter list named for it,
# and writable is in the reduced OpenBSD one too.
# writable.letters is one id for every target the payload plants into, grouped
# the way names.sh and pinfloor.sh group: the sentence carries the target and
# the id carries the claim. The expected set is per-platform and each lane holds
# its own, so this cell going red means one letter moved somewhere -- measured
# by flipping the Linux set's `home` to writable, which turns it red on one of
# six and leaves the rest green.
# Two of these can be skipped rather than failed, and both are exemptions that
